title: Epistolae Et Decreta
author: Pelagius II
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1243.tmp1243.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: Nujus epistolæ meminit beatus Gregorius lib. II, tpist. 36, ad episcopos Hiberniæ, quam librum appellat. Eam ab eodem beato Gregorio, cum adhuc esset diaconus, scriptam fuisse nomine Pelagii papæ, testatur Paulut Warnefridus lib. III de Gestis Langobardorum, cap. 10, a!. 20.
passages.english: Blessed Gregory mentions this letter in Book II, Letter 36, to the bishops of Ireland, where he calls it a "book." Paul Warnefrid, in Book III of the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 10 (elsewhere 20), testifies that it was written by that same blessed Gregory, while he was still a deacon, in the name of Pope Pelagius.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "Nujus" read as "Hujus", "tpist." as "epist.", "Paulut" as "Paulus", "a!." as "al." (alias, i.e. an alternative chapter numbering). Paul Warnefrid is Paul the Deacon. "Hiberniæ" is rendered "Ireland", though the letter's actual addressees may be disputed.

passages.original: et plus in hæreticis sensum proprium, quam testatio Eusebii absolvere potuit, nec rursum Eusebium laudati Origenis culpa damnavit. An non et Gregorius Nyssae urbis episcopus cum Canticum canticorum exponit, magnis Origenem laudibus præferi ? An non et Hieronymus nostræ Ecclesiae presbyter, et singularis Hebraei sermonis interpres, tanto erga Origenem favore intenditur, ut pene discipulus ejus esse videatur? Sed quia plus causa quam verba pensanda sunt, nec itis sua benignitas nocuit, nec illum a reatu proprio favor alienae attestationis excusavit.
passages.english: and Origen's own way of thinking among heretics weighed more than Eusebius' testimony could acquit, nor, in turn, did the guilt of the Origen he praised condemn Eusebius. Does not Gregory too, bishop of the city of Nyssa, when he expounds the Song of Songs, set Origen forward with great praise? Does not Jerome too, presbyter of our Church and a singular interpreter of the Hebrew tongue, bend himself to Origen with such favour that he almost seems to be his disciple? But because the case must be weighed more than the words, neither did their kindness harm these men, nor did the favour of another's testimony excuse that man from his own guilt.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening 'et plus...' continues a clause from the preceding context (the Church weighs hearts more kindly than words strictly), so the subject of 'weighed more' is supplied by sense. 'præferi' read as 'præfert' (scanning error). 'nec itis' read as 'nec istis' ('these men', i.e. Gregory and Jerome). 'delcrius' in the context is evidently 'deterius'.
